rationale: Across published cohorts of autosomal recessive intellectual developmental disorder 84 (MRT84, OMIM #620401) caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in SGSM3, exactly 15 molecularly confirmed patients have been described in peer-reviewed literature. Birnbaum et al. (2024) reported 13 affected individuals from 8 unrelated families of Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry who all share the identical homozygous frameshift founder variant. Turkyilmaz et al. (2025) reported 2 affected siblings from a different population who harbor a novel homozygous nonsense variant (c.1576C>T, p.Arg526Ter). With 13 out of 15 confirmed individuals harboring the Ashkenazi Jewish founder variant, it represents 86.7% of all currently published MRT84 cases worldwide, well above the 70% threshold stated in the hypothesis.

evidence.text: Birnbaum et al. identified 13 individuals from 8 families of Ashkenazi Jewish origin who all carry the identical homozygous frameshift founder variant in SGSM3, presenting with mild global developmental delay, mild to moderate intellectual disability, hypotonia, behavioral challenges, and short stature.

new_directions.question_text: How many unreported or non-Ashkenazi MRT84 patients currently exist in large international intellectual disability/autism sequencing registries such as GeneMatcher, Decipher, and Solve-RD?
new_directions.rationale: Because MRT84 was only recently described, ascertainment bias toward Ashkenazi carrier screening and consanguineous families may artificially elevate the proportion accounted for by the founder allele.

new_directions.question_text: Does the phenotypic expression of MRT84 differ between individuals carrying the C-terminal stop-gain variant (p.Arg526Ter) and the upstream frameshift founder variant?
new_directions.rationale: Comparing the clinical manifestations across both molecularly confirmed cohorts will clarify whether syndromic features like dysmorphisms or behavioral disturbances correlate with specific truncation locations or escape from nonsense-mediated decay.
